question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

OBDURATE
option_1: Compliant
option_2: Pliant
option_3: Unyielding
option_4: Amenable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Unyielding.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Obdurate (adjective) means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action; hardened against persuasion. (हठी, कठोर)
◦ Example: The management remained obdurate despite three rounds of talks.

 

• Unyielding means refusing to bend, give way or be persuaded, which is exactly the sense required. (अटल, न झुकने वाला)
◦ Example: She met the accusation with unyielding calm.

 

• The word comes from Latin obduratus, 'hardened' — the same root as durable and endure, all carrying the idea of hardness.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Compliant (आज्ञाकारी): inclined to agree with others or obey rules — an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Pliant (लचीला, नरम): easily influenced or bent — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Amenable (सहमत होने योग्य): open to suggestion, easily persuaded — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of obdurate: obstinate, intransigent, adamant, inflexible, implacable.

 

• Note the useful distinction: adamant stresses firmness of will, obdurate adds a shade of hard-heartedness.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

INTREPID
option_1: Fearless
option_2: Timid
option_3: Apprehensive
option_4: Cowardly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Fearless.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Intrepid (adjective) means fearless and adventurous, especially in the face of danger. (निडर, साहसी)
◦ Example: The intrepid climbers reached the summit in a blizzard.

 

• Fearless conveys precisely this quality — showing no fear. (निर्भय)
◦ Example: Her fearless reporting from the conflict zone won an award.

 

• The word is built from Latin in- ('not') + trepidus ('alarmed'), so it literally means 'not alarmed'. The same root survives in trepidation, meaning fear or nervousness.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Timid (डरपोक): lacking courage or confidence — an antonym.

 

• Option 3: Apprehensive (आशंकित): anxious that something bad may happen — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Cowardly (कायर): lacking the courage to face danger — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of intrepid: dauntless, undaunted, valiant, audacious, gallant.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

NADIR
option_1: Trough
option_2: Depth
option_3: Bottom
option_4: Zenith
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Zenith.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nadir (noun) means the lowest point in the fortunes of a person or organisation; in astronomy, the point of the sky directly below an observer. (निम्नतम बिंदु, पराकाष्ठा का उलट)
◦ Example: The party reached its nadir after losing every seat in the state.

 

• Its exact opposite is zenith — the highest point; the peak of success or power. (शिखर, चरम बिंदु)
◦ Example: The empire was at its zenith under that ruler.

 

• The remaining three options all denote low points, so they are synonyms of the given word and can be eliminated together.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Trough (गर्त): the lowest part of a wave or of an economic cycle — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Depth (गहराई): used in expressions such as 'the depths of despair' — a synonym in this sense.

 

• Option 3: Bottom (तल): the lowest part of anything — a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of nadir: apex, pinnacle, summit, acme, apogee, culmination.

 

• Both nadir and zenith entered English from Arabic through medieval astronomy — a pair worth memorising together.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

Hobson's choice
option_1: A choice between two equally unpleasant alternatives
option_2: An apparently free choice in which only one option is actually offered
option_3: A decision taken hastily and later regretted
option_4: A decision deliberately left to somebody else
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. An apparently free choice in which only one option is actually offered.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Hobson's choice' means a situation in which one appears to be given a choice, but in fact only a single option is available — take it or leave it. (नाममात्र का विकल्प; वस्तुतः कोई विकल्प न होना)
◦ Example: With only one bidder left, the board faced a Hobson's choice.

 

• The phrase comes from Thomas Hobson, a Cambridge stable-keeper who let out horses strictly in rotation: a customer could take the horse nearest the door or take none at all.

 

• The essential idea is therefore the absence of a real alternative, not the unpleasantness of the alternatives.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes a dilemma or Morton's fork — two options, both bad. This is the commonest confusion in the exam.

 

• Option 3 would suit 'to act in haste and repent at leisure'.

 

• Option 4 describes delegation and has no connection with the idiom.

 

NOTE

 

• Related expressions of constrained choice: between the devil and the deep sea, between a rock and a hard place, on the horns of a dilemma, no choice in the matter.

question: Choose the correct spelling of a word meaning 'writing paper, envelopes and other office materials'.
option_1: Stationery
option_2: Stationary
option_3: Stationnery
option_4: Stationairy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Stationery.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Stationery (noun) means paper, envelopes, pens and similar writing materials. (लेखन सामग्री)
◦ Example: The office ordered fresh stationery for the new session.

 

• The decisive letter is the e in the last syllable: station-e-ry. A simple memory aid is that stationEry contains E for Envelope, while stationAry contains A for At rest.

 

• Stationary (Option 2) is a real word but a different one — an adjective meaning not moving. (स्थिर)
◦ Example: The train remained stationary for an hour outside the junction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 3: Stationnery — wrong; the n has been needlessly doubled.

 

• Option 4: Stationairy — wrong; an intrusive ai has replaced the single vowel.

 

NOTE

 

• Pairs distinguished by a single vowel: stationery/stationary, complement/compliment, dependant/dependent, affect/effect.

 

• Noun/verb pairs distinguished by c and s in British usage: licence/license, practice/practise, advice/advise, prophecy/prophesy.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word for 'a violation or misuse of something regarded as sacred'.
option_1: Sacrilage
option_2: Sacrelige
option_3: Sacriledge
option_4: Sacrilege
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Sacrilege.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sacrilege (noun) means the violation or profanation of anything held sacred. (पवित्र वस्तु का अपमान, धर्मद्रोह)
◦ Example: Removing the inscription was condemned as an act of sacrilege.

 

• The correct division is SAC - RI - LEGE. Two traps must be avoided:
◦ the second vowel is i, not e — sacrilege;
◦ the ending is -lege, never -ledge, even though the word is pronounced as though it were.

 

• It comes from Latin sacrilegium, formed from sacer ('sacred') and legere ('to gather, to steal') — literally the stealing of sacred things.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Sacrilage — wrong; the ending has been written -lage.

 

• Option 2: Sacrelige — wrong; the vowels i and e have been transposed.

 

• Option 3: Sacriledge — wrong; a d has been inserted before the ending on the strength of the pronunciation.

 

NOTE

 

• The adjective is sacrilegious, which is itself among the most frequently misspelt words in English — note that it is not spelt like 'religious'.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitution for: 'A person who is indifferent or hostile to art, literature and culture'.
option_1: Aesthete
option_2: Philistine
option_3: Connoisseur
option_4: Virtuoso
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Philistine.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A philistine is a person who is smugly indifferent or openly hostile to art, literature and intellectual pursuits. (कलाविमुख, असंस्कृत व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: He dismissed the entire exhibition in a sentence, like the philistine he was.

 

• The word derives from the Philistines of the ancient Near East, who were represented in later European writing as uncultured adversaries of learning.

 

• The other three options all denote people with a high regard for art, which is the opposite of what the definition requires.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Aesthete (सौंदर्यप्रेमी): a person with a special appreciation of beauty and art.

 

• Option 3: Connoisseur (पारखी): an expert judge in matters of taste, such as art, food or wine.

 

• Option 4: Virtuoso (निपुण कलाकार): a person of outstanding technical skill, especially in music.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the difference between connoisseur (one who judges with expert taste) and virtuoso (one who performs with exceptional skill).

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'To renounce a throne or high office formally'.
option_1: Abrogate
option_2: Abjure
option_3: Abdicate
option_4: Absolve
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Abdicate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abdicate (verb) means to give up a throne, high office or responsibility formally. (सिंहासन या पद त्यागना)
◦ Example: The king abdicated in favour of his younger brother.

 

• The word joins Latin ab- ('away') and dicare ('to proclaim') — to proclaim oneself away from office.

 

• All four options begin with ab- and are deliberately chosen to look alike; only the second element of each word separates them.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Abrogate (रद्द करना): to repeal or annul a law, treaty or agreement.

 

• Option 2: Abjure (शपथपूर्वक त्यागना): to renounce a belief, claim or oath solemnly.

 

• Option 4: Absolve (दोषमुक्त करना): to declare somebody free from guilt, blame or obligation.

 

NOTE

 

• Abdicate is also used figuratively — *The board has abdicated its responsibility to the shareholders.*

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

He orders the staff about as if he _____ the owner of the firm.
option_1: is
option_2: were
option_3: was
option_4: has been
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. were.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The conjunctions as if and as though introduce a comparison with something unreal or contrary to fact. In such clauses English uses the past subjunctive, and the subjunctive form of 'be' is were for every subject — I, he, she, it included.
◦ Example: She speaks as if she knew the whole story.

 

• Here the man is not the owner; the clause merely compares his manner with that of an owner. The unreal comparison therefore requires were, not is or was.

 

• The completed sentence: He orders the staff about as if he were the owner of the firm.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: is — the indicative would assert that he really is the owner, contradicting the sense of 'as if'.

 

• Option 3: was — common in informal speech and not condemned by all grammarians, but in formal written English, which the exam follows, the subjunctive were is the required form; the question asks for the most appropriate option.

 

• Option 4: has been — the present perfect has no place in an unreal comparison.

 

NOTE

 

• Were is likewise used after wish and if only in unreal statements: *I wish I were taller; If only he were here.*

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The chairman was accompanied (1)/ with two senior directors (2)/ when he addressed (3)/ the press conference yesterday. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb accompany takes by when the companion is a person, and with only when what is added is a thing.
◦ Example (person): The minister was accompanied by his secretary.
◦ Example (thing): The main dish was accompanied with a green salad.

 

• Here the companions are two senior directors — persons — so part (2) must read 'by two senior directors'.

 

• The corrected sentence: The chairman was accompanied by two senior directors when he addressed the press conference yesterday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: the passive was accompanied rightly agrees with the singular subject The chairman.

 

• Part (3) and Part (4) are sound; addressed correctly takes the direct object the press conference, and yesterday fixes the simple past.

 

NOTE

 

• Similar preposition traps in the passive: surrounded by (people) / surrounded with (things), filled with (never 'filled by' for contents), known to a person but known for a quality.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If I would have known (1)/ about the sudden change in schedule, (2)/ I would certainly have informed (3)/ the rest of the team in advance. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a third conditional, the if-clause takes the past perfect and the main clause takes would have + past participle. The auxiliary would never appears in the if-clause of a conditional.

 

• Part (1) must therefore read 'If I had known'. The structure is:
◦ If + had + V3 ... would have + V3

 

• The corrected sentence: If I had known about the sudden change in schedule, I would certainly have informed the rest of the team in advance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (3) is correct — would certainly have informed is the proper main-clause form; the adverb may stand between the auxiliaries.

 

• The same sentence may be written with inversion and no 'if': *Had I known about the sudden change in schedule, I would certainly have informed the rest of the team.*

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the rule as 'no would in the if'. The same applies to the second conditional: *If I were you* — never 'If I would be you'.

question:
Change the following from active to passive.

 

The workers are repairing the damaged bridge.
option_1: The damaged bridge is repaired by the workers.
option_2: The damaged bridge was being repaired by the workers.
option_3: The damaged bridge has been repaired by the workers.
option_4: The damaged bridge is being repaired by the workers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The damaged bridge is being repaired by the workers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active sentence is in the present continuous tense (are repairing). The passive of the present continuous is formed as:
◦ is/am/are + being + past participle (V3)

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ The object the damaged bridge becomes the subject; being singular, it takes is.
◦ are repairing → is being repaired.
◦ The subject the workers becomes the agent introduced by by.

 

• Note that the auxiliary agrees with the new subject, so the plural are of the active becomes the singular is in the passive.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 gives the simple present passive and loses the sense of an action in progress.

 

• Option 2 shifts the action into the past continuous.

 

• Option 3 gives the present perfect passive, which would mean the work is finished.

 

NOTE

 

• The word being is the mark of a continuous passive: *is being done, was being done*. There is no accepted passive for the perfect continuous tenses.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

Let the windows be closed before the storm reaches the coast.
option_1: The windows should be closed before the storm reaches the coast.
option_2: You are closing the windows before the storm reaches the coast.
option_3: Somebody closes the windows before the storm reaches the coast.
option_4: Close the windows before the storm reaches the coast.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Close the windows before the storm reaches the coast.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pattern 'Let + object + be + past participle' is the passive form of an imperative sentence — a command or instruction.

 

• To restore the active voice, the imperative is simply given back its ordinary form: verb + object, with the subject 'you' understood.
◦ Passive: Let the file be submitted at once. → Active: Submit the file at once.

 

• Applying this here gives 'Close the windows', and the time clause 'before the storm reaches the coast' stays untouched.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is still passive and, by replacing the command with should, weakens it into advice.

 

• Option 2 turns it into a present continuous description, not an instruction.

 

• Option 3 turns the command into a statement of fact about somebody.

 

NOTE

 

• Imperatives in the passive follow two patterns: Let + object + be + V3 for positive commands, and Let not + object + be + V3 (or 'Let ... not be ...') for negative ones.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word.

 

The contractor submitted a tender for the road-widening project.
option_1: The lowest tender was accepted by the municipal board.
option_2: Her voice was low and unexpectedly tender.
option_3: Several firms filed a tender before the closing date.
option_4: The tender documents ran to nearly forty pages.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Her voice was low and unexpectedly tender.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word identical in spelling and pronunciation to another but carrying a completely different meaning. (समनामी शब्द)

 

• In the given sentence tender is a noun meaning a formal written offer to supply goods or carry out work at a stated price. The question therefore asks for the sentence in which the same word carries a different meaning.

 

• Option 2 uses tender as an adjective meaning gentle, soft or affectionate. The description of a voice as 'low and unexpectedly tender' fixes this second sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1, Option 3 and Option 4 all use tender in the same commercial sense as the highlighted word, so none of them qualifies as a homonym.

 

• Tender has a third life as a verb meaning 'to offer formally' — *He tendered his resignation* — and appears in the phrase legal tender, meaning currency that must be accepted in payment.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the three terms apart: homonyms are alike in spelling and sound (tender, bat, spell); homophones sound alike but are spelt differently (stationary/stationery, air/heir); homographs are spelt alike but may be pronounced differently (lead, tear, sow).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The professor explained us the theorem twice before the examination.
option_1: explained us about the theorem
option_2: explained to us about the theorem
option_3: explained the theorem to us
option_4: explained us of the theorem
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. explained the theorem to us.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Explain is a verb that takes a direct object (the thing explained) and introduces the person with the preposition to. The fixed pattern is explain something to somebody. (समझाना)
◦ Example: Please explain the rule to the new members.

 

• It can never take a person as its immediate object. 'Explained us the theorem' is therefore wrong, however natural it may sound by analogy with 'told us the answer'.

 

• The corrected sentence: The professor explained the theorem to us twice before the examination.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: explained us about the theorem — retains the person as object and adds a needless about.

 

• Option 2: explained to us about the theorem — the preposition to is now right, but about is superfluous before a definite thing.

 

• Option 4: explained us of the theorem — of is not used with this verb at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs that behave like explain and require to before the person: suggest, describe, announce, propose, mention, recommend, report, dictate. Contrast tell, give, offer, send, which take the person directly.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Every society needs some way of deciding who shall be admitted to what, and the written examination has for two centuries been the least objectionable answer available. Its virtues are not trivial. It is blind to the candidate's family, indifferent to his accent, and cheap enough to be administered to millions on the same morning. Where patronage once decided appointments, a mark-sheet now does, and the change was, on any reasonable accounting, an advance.

 

The difficulty begins when the instrument is mistaken for the thing it measures. An examination can test what a candidate has learnt to reproduce under time pressure; it cannot test judgement, persistence or the capacity to work with others, and it makes no attempt to. Yet the score it yields is treated as a verdict on the whole person, and candidates soon learn to behave accordingly. Preparation ceases to be the study of a subject and becomes the study of a paper — its recurring patterns, its scoring conventions, its favourite traps. A coaching industry grows up to teach precisely this, and the more efficiently it teaches, the less the examination reveals about anything except the ability to pay for coaching.

 

Nor is the fairness of the instrument as complete as it appears. The examination is impartial at the moment of assessment, but it says nothing about the eighteen years that preceded that moment. Two candidates who sit the same paper may have arrived at it from a well-equipped city school and from a village school without a science teacher, and the marks will faithfully record the difference in their preparation while concealing its cause. Impartiality at the last step can thus lend an appearance of desert to an outcome that was largely settled earlier.

 

None of this is an argument for abolishing examinations, and the alternatives usually proposed — interviews, recommendations, continuous assessment — are more easily manipulated, not less. It is an argument for holding the examination to its proper scale: a rough, useful and necessarily incomplete instrument, worth defending against those who would replace it with patronage, and worth doubting whenever it is spoken of as though it measured merit itself.

 

What is the central argument of the passage?
option_1: The examination is a useful but limited instrument that should not be mistaken for a measure of merit itself.
option_2: Examinations are wholly fair because they treat every candidate alike.
option_3: Examinations should be replaced by interviews and continuous assessment.
option_4: The coaching industry alone is responsible for the failings of the examination system.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The examination is a useful but limited instrument that should not be mistaken for a measure of merit itself.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage opens by defending the examination — it is 'blind to the candidate's family', cheap, and better than the patronage it replaced — and then sets out its limits: it cannot test judgement or persistence, and it conceals the inequality of the years before it.

 

• The closing sentence states the thesis outright: the examination is 'a rough, useful and necessarily incomplete instrument ... worth doubting whenever it is spoken of as though it measured merit itself.'

 

• A main-idea answer must hold both halves together — the defence and the doubt — and only Option 1 does so.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 ignores the entire third paragraph on unequal preparation.

 

• Option 3 is expressly rejected: the alternatives 'are more easily manipulated, not less'.

 

• Option 4 inflates one illustration — the coaching industry — into the whole argument.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage both praises and criticises the same thing, the correct main-idea option almost always contains a qualifier such as 'useful but limited'; options that praise or condemn without qualification are traps.

It is an argument for holding the examination to its proper scale: a rough, useful and necessarily incomplete instrument, worth defending against those who would replace it with patronage, and worth doubting whenever it is spoken of as though it measured merit itself.

 

What does the author mean by 'the instrument is mistaken for the thing it measures'?
option_1: A narrow test score is treated as a judgement on the whole person.
option_2: The examination paper is often printed with errors in it.
option_3: Candidates confuse one subject with another while preparing.
option_4: Examiners are unable to measure answers accurately.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A narrow test score is treated as a judgement on the whole person.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence immediately following the phrase supplies its meaning: an examination 'can test what a candidate has learnt to reproduce under time pressure; it cannot test judgement, persistence or the capacity to work with others' — and yet 'the score it yields is treated as a verdict on the whole person.'

 

• The instrument is therefore the examination, and the thing it measures is the far larger quality — merit or worth — that people imagine it to capture.

 

• To mistake one for the other is to let a narrow measurement stand in for a whole judgement, which is exactly what Option 1 states.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 reads 'instrument' as the physical question paper and misses the figurative sense.

 

• Option 3 describes a mistake by candidates, whereas the author is describing a mistake by society.

 

• Option 4 concerns the accuracy of marking, which the passage never questions — it questions what the mark means.

 

NOTE

 

• For 'what does the author mean by' questions, read the sentence immediately before and after the quoted phrase; the explanation is nearly always adjacent to it.

According to the passage, what happens to preparation once the score is treated as a verdict?
option_1: It shifts from written work to oral practice.
option_2: It is abandoned altogether by most candidates.
option_3: It becomes the study of the paper's patterns and conventions rather than of the subject.
option_4: It becomes cheaper and more widely available.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. It becomes the study of the paper's patterns and conventions rather than of the subject.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states: 'Preparation ceases to be the study of a subject and becomes the study of a paper — its recurring patterns, its scoring conventions, its favourite traps.'

 

• The author then draws the consequence: a coaching industry grows up to teach exactly this, and 'the more efficiently it teaches, the less the examination reveals about anything except the ability to pay for coaching.'

 

• The change described is therefore one of object of study — from subject to paper.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces oral practice, a topic absent from the passage.

 

• Option 2 overstates the case; the passage says preparation changes in kind, not that it stops.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the passage, which links coaching to the ability to pay.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the author's use of the dash to expand a phrase: 'the study of a paper — its recurring patterns ...'. Such expansions frequently supply the wording of the correct option.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Every society needs some way of deciding who shall be admitted to what, and the written examination has for two centuries been the least objectionable answer available. Its virtues are not trivial. It is blind to the candidate's family, indifferent to his accent, and cheap enough to be administered to millions on the same morning. Where patronage once decided appointments, a mark-sheet now does, and the change was, on any reasonable accounting, an advance.

 

The difficulty begins when the instrument is mistaken for the thing it measures. An examination can test what a candidate has learnt to reproduce under time pressure; it cannot test judgement, persistence or the capacity to work with others, and it makes no attempt to. Yet the score it yields is treated as a verdict on the whole person, and candidates soon learn to behave accordingly. Preparation ceases to be the study of a subject and becomes the study of a paper — its recurring patterns, its scoring conventions, its favourite traps. A coaching industry grows up to teach precisely this, and the more efficiently it teaches, the less the examination reveals about anything except the ability to pay for coaching.

 

Nor is the fairness of the instrument as complete as it appears. The examination is impartial at the moment of assessment, but it says nothing about the eighteen years that preceded that moment. Two candidates who sit the same paper may have arrived at it from a well-equipped city school and from a village school without a science teacher, and the marks will faithfully record the difference in their preparation while concealing its cause. Impartiality at the last step can thus lend an appearance of desert to an outcome that was largely settled earlier.

 

None of this is an argument for abolishing examinations, and the alternatives usually proposed — interviews, recommendations, continuous assessment — are more easily manipulated, not less. It is an argument for holding the examination to its proper scale: a rough, useful and necessarily incomplete instrument, worth defending against those who would replace it with patronage, and worth doubting whenever it is spoken of as though it measured merit itself.

 

Why does the author mention a village school without a science teacher?
option_1: To argue that rural schools should be closed and merged.
option_2: To show that impartiality at the moment of assessment does not undo the inequality that preceded it.
option_3: To explain why science subjects are harder to examine than others.
option_4: To prove that examinations should be conducted in every village.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To show that impartiality at the moment of assessment does not undo the inequality that preceded it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The example appears in the paragraph beginning 'Nor is the fairness of the instrument as complete as it appears.' Its function is to place two candidates side by side — one from a well-equipped city school, one from a village school — who sit the same paper.

 

• The author's conclusion follows at once: the marks 'will faithfully record the difference in their preparation while concealing its cause', so that 'impartiality at the last step can thus lend an appearance of desert to an outcome that was largely settled earlier.'

 

• The illustration therefore serves an argument about fairness over time, not an argument about rural schooling as such.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 proposes a policy on school mergers that the passage never touches.

 

• Option 3 shifts the point to the difficulty of examining science, which is not discussed.

 

• Option 4 confuses the location of schools with the location of examination centres.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Why does the author mention X' questions ask for the function of a detail. Identify the claim the paragraph is making, and choose the option that shows X supporting that claim.

It is an argument for holding the examination to its proper scale: a rough, useful and necessarily incomplete instrument, worth defending against those who would replace it with patronage, and worth doubting whenever it is spoken of as though it measured merit itself.

 

Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?
option_1: Dismissive and cynical
option_2: Indignant and polemical
option_3: Nostalgic and sentimental
option_4: Balanced and analytical
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Balanced and analytical.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The author concedes the merits of the examination before stating its limits — 'Its virtues are not trivial', 'the change was, on any reasonable accounting, an advance' — and expressly refuses the extreme position: 'None of this is an argument for abolishing examinations.'

 

• At the same time the argument is analytical: it distinguishes the instrument from what it is taken to measure, and separates fairness at the moment of assessment from fairness over the preceding years.

 

• Weighing both sides and reaching a qualified conclusion is precisely what is meant by a balanced and analytical tone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Dismissive and cynical — the author defends the examination against those who would replace it with patronage, so nothing is dismissed.

 

• Option 2: Indignant and polemical — the writing is measured and qualified, with none of the heat of a polemic.

 

• Option 3: Nostalgic and sentimental — there is no longing for the past; the past here means patronage, which the author considers worse.

 

NOTE

 

• For tone questions, look at the adjectives and qualifiers an author chooses. Words such as 'rough', 'useful', 'necessarily incomplete' signal measured judgement; words such as 'outrageous' or 'disgraceful' would signal indignation.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said, “I was waiting for the bus.”
option_1: He said that he is waiting for the bus.
option_2: He said that he has been waiting for the bus.
option_3: He said that he had been waiting for the bus.
option_4: He said that he would wait for the bus.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. He said that he had been waiting for the bus.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported words are in the past continuous (was waiting). After a past reporting verb this backshifts to the past perfect continuous:
◦ was/were + V-ing → had been + V-ing

 

• The pronoun I becomes he, and the conjunction that is supplied.

 

• The completed sentence: He said that he had been waiting for the bus.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the present continuous, so no backshift has taken place at all.

 

• Option 2 uses the present perfect continuous, which likewise cannot follow the past reporting verb 'said'.

 

• Option 4 replaces a continuous action with a future intention and alters the meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• The full backshift table: simple present → simple past; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect → past perfect; simple past → past perfect; past continuous → past perfect continuous. The past perfect itself does not change further.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to his friends, “Let us go for a walk along the river.”
option_1: He told his friends to go for a walk along the river.
option_2: He asked his friends whether they went for a walk along the river.
option_3: He said to his friends that let them go for a walk along the river.
option_4: He suggested to his friends that they should go for a walk along the river.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He suggested to his friends that they should go for a walk along the river.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Let us' at the beginning of a quoted sentence expresses a proposal or suggestion that includes the speaker. In indirect speech the reporting verb becomes suggested or proposed, followed by that + subject + should.
◦ Example: He said, 'Let us begin.' → He suggested that they should begin.

 

• The pronoun us covers the speaker together with the listeners, so it becomes a third-person plural; and because it is the subject of the that-clause it takes the nominative form they, not 'them'.

 

• The completed sentence: He suggested to his friends that they should go for a walk along the river.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 converts the proposal into an order and excludes the speaker, who was to walk with them.

 

• Option 2 turns a suggestion into a question about the past.

 

• Option 3 keeps the word let inside a that-clause, which is not permitted in reported speech.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish the two uses of 'let': 'Let us go' (a suggestion → *suggested that ... should*) from 'Let him go' (permission or a passive imperative → *requested that he might be allowed to go* / *ordered that he should be let go*).

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

He requested me to lend him my notes for a day.
option_1: He said to me, “Please lend me your notes for a day.”
option_2: He said to me, “Please lend him your notes for a day.”
option_3: He said to me, “Please lend me his notes for a day.”
option_4: He said to me, “You please lent me your notes for a day.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He said to me, “Please lend me your notes for a day.”

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb requested shows that the quoted words were a polite request. Converting back to direct speech requires three changes:
◦ requested becomes said to, and the words are placed within inverted commas;
◦ the to-infinitive returns to the imperative, softened by please;
◦ the pronouns are restored from the speaker's point of view.

 

• Working through the pronouns: him refers to the speaker, so it becomes me; my notes belong to the listener, so they become your notes.

 

• The reconstructed sentence is therefore: He said to me, “Please lend me your notes for a day.”

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps him, which would make the speaker ask for the notes on behalf of a third person.

 

• Option 3 keeps his notes, reversing the ownership stated in the indirect version.

 

• Option 4 uses the past form lent where the imperative lend is required.

 

NOTE

 

• Reporting verbs and their direct forms: requested → 'Please ...', ordered/commanded → plain imperative, advised → 'You had better ...', forbade → 'Do not ...', invited → 'Will you ...?'

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph.

 

1. Monsoon forecasting in India rests on two quite different methods.
2. Forecasters therefore publish a range of values rather than a single confident figure.
3. The statistical method compares the present year with the long historical record.
4. The dynamical method, by contrast, solves the equations of atmospheric motion on a supercomputer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 1-3-4-2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 1 is the opening: it names the subject — monsoon forecasting — and announces that two methods will follow. A sentence that promises a list must precede the list.

 

• Sentence 3 gives the first of the two methods, the statistical one.

 

• Sentence 4 gives the second, and the phrase 'by contrast' confirms that it must follow the method it is being contrasted with.

 

• Sentence 2 is the conclusion, marked by 'therefore', drawing the consequence of having two imperfect methods.

 

• The chain is thus announcement → first method → second method → consequence: 1-3-4-2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (3-4-1-2) begins with a method before the reader is told that two methods exist.

 

• Option 3 (1-4-3-2) places the 'by contrast' sentence before the method it is contrasted with, so sentence 4 has nothing to stand against but the announcement.

 

• Option 4 (4-3-1-2) opens with 'by contrast' before either method has been named, so it cannot begin this self-contained paragraph.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence announcing a number — 'two methods', 'three stages', 'several reasons' — almost always opens the paragraph, and the items follow in order.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage.

 

1. Therefore any effort to save the species must begin with the grasslands themselves.
2. The Great Indian Bustard is among the most threatened birds of the subcontinent.
3. It nests on open ground and lays only a single egg at a time.
4. Loss of grassland and collision with overhead power lines have together reduced its numbers drastically.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-3-4-1.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 opens the paragraph: it names the subject — the Great Indian Bustard — and states the general fact about it. No other sentence introduces the bird by name.

 

• Sentence 3 follows with its breeding habits; the pronoun 'It' requires the named subject of sentence 2 immediately before it.

 

• Sentence 4 supplies the causes of decline, which build on the vulnerability implied by ground-nesting and a single egg.

 

• Sentence 1 is the conclusion, signalled by 'Therefore', and its reference to 'the grasslands' presupposes that grassland loss has already been mentioned in sentence 4.

 

• The order is therefore subject → habit → threat → conclusion: 2-3-4-1.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (3-2-4-1) opens with the pronoun 'It', which has no antecedent.

 

• Option 3 (2-4-3-1) separates the conclusion about grasslands from the sentence that first mentions grassland loss.

 

• Option 4 (4-2-3-1) begins with the threats before the species has been named.

 

NOTE

 

• Two reliable rules for this question type: a pronoun cannot appear before the noun it stands for, and a sentence beginning with Therefore, Hence or Thus almost always comes last.
